extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in discrete mathematics/introduction to proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, equivalences, and translation/negation/inference principles for introductory symbolic logic and basic counting (lists). Intended to guide translating English mathematics into symbols, building truth tables, negating quantified/conditional statements, and simple counting via the multiplication principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse vs original implication
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P are generally different statements; the converse Q ⇒ P need not follow from P ⇒ Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (a is even) ⇒ (a divisible by 2) is true and its converse (a divisible by 2) ⇒ (a is even) is also true here, but in general one should not assume the converse holds. The converse of a conditional is called its 'converse.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional meaning (P ⇔ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇔ Q is defined to mean (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P); read 'P if and only if Q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently P ⇔ Q holds exactly when P and Q are both true or both false. English paraphrases include 'P is a necessary and sufficient condition for Q' and 'If P, then Q, and conversely.' Example: (a is even) ⇔ (a is divisible by 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth table construction for compound statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate a compound statement build a truth table listing all combinations of component truth values and compute columns for subexpressions as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helper columns for intermediate expressions (e.g., P∨Q, P∧Q, ¬(P∧Q)) are useful and may be omitted when confident. Example given for (P∨Q)∧¬(P∧Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive or as formula
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement 'one but not both of P and Q is true' can be expressed as (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula is true precisely when exactly one of P or Q is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses and operator precedence (negation binding)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negation symbol ¬ (or ∼) negates the expression it immediately precedes; ¬P ∨ Q means (¬P) ∨ Q, not ¬(P ∨ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negating a whole parenthesized expression use ¬( ... ). Be careful with precedence when mixing operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional equivalence to disjunction of conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇔ Q is logically equivalent to (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify by truth table; this shows P ⇔ Q is true when P and Q share the same truth value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive equivalence (contrapositive law)
rubrics_metrics.description: P ⇒ Q is logically equivalent to (¬Q) ⇒ (¬P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence can make proofs easier by proving the contrapositive instead of the original implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's laws
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth tables or intuition: 'not (both P and Q)' means 'at least one is false', etc. Useful for negating conjunctions/disjunctions and simplifying negations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard logical equivalences (algebraic laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commutative, associative, and distributive laws for ∧ and ∨ (e.g., P ∧ Q = Q ∧ P; P ∧ (Q ∨ R) = (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R)), and associativity allowing omission of parentheses for repeated same operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities mirror algebraic laws and can be verified by truth tables. Parentheses can be dropped for associative chains (e.g., P ∧ Q ∧ R), but are essential when mixing ∧ and ∨.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth values match line-for-line in a truth table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalences allow rewriting statements into potentially more convenient forms (e.g., P ⇒ Q = (¬P) ∨ Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication truth condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional 'If P then Q' is true if it is impossible for P to be true while Q is false; it is false exactly when P is true and Q is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise truth-table-based meaning of 'If..., then...' used in mathematics, and must be internalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied universal quantifier for unquantified conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, a conditional P(x) ⇒ Q(x) about elements of some set S is understood as the statement ∀ x ∈ S, P(x) ⇒ Q(x) unless a different quantifier is specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because universal conditionals are so common, the ∀ is often omitted in writing but implied; be aware when interpreting or negating such statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal quantifier (∀) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ∀ x ∈ S, P(x) is true iff P(x) holds for every x ∈ S; false if there exists at least one x ∈ S with P(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∀ n ∈ Z, 2n is even. Use truth tables or examples to test universal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier (∃) meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ∃ x ∈ S, P(x) is true iff there exists at least one x ∈ S for which P(x) is true; otherwise false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∃ X ⊆ {1,...,n}, |X| = 5. Provide a witness to show existential statements true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple quantifiers occur, changing their order generally changes meaning (e.g., ∀x ∃y versus ∃y ∀x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: ∀x ∃y y^3 = x (true) vs ∃y ∀x y^3 = x (false). Always pay attention to quantifier order when translating or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations: 'and', 'or', 'but' in English to logic
rubrics_metrics.description: 'But' can be rendered as 'and'; 'and' in English does not always translate to ∧ when meaning is actually 'at least one' (use ∨).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At least one of the integers x and y is even.' should be (x is even) ∨ (y is even), not (x is even) ∧ (y is even). 'The integer x is even, but the integer y is odd' is (x even) ∧ (y odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of quantifiers (rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negations swap quantifiers: ¬(∀ x ∈ S, P(x)) = ∃ x ∈ S, ¬P(x); ¬(∃ x ∈ S, P(x)) = ∀ x ∈ S, ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these when forming logical negations of quantified statements. Example: negation of 'every real has a cube root' yields 'there exists a real with no cube root.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of a conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: ¬(P ⇒ Q) is logically equivalent to P ∧ ¬Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because P⇒Q is false only when P is true and Q false. Use this when negating universally quantified conditionals by combining with quantifier negation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English mathematical statements into symbolic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing proofs or interpreting theorems, translate sentences carefully into symbolic form to reveal logical structure; don't mechanically replace words without checking meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include translating the Mean Value Theorem, Goldbach's conjecture, and careful handling of 'not all' vs 'all not' (e.g., 'All integers are not even' is wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of truth tables to verify equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Less obvious equivalences should be verified with truth tables by comparing columns line-by-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several exercises ask to verify equivalences (distributive/DeMorgan/conditional identities) with truth tables; building helper columns is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical inference patterns (rules of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common valid inference patterns include: modus ponens (P ⇒ Q, P ⊢ Q); modus tollens (P ⇒ Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P); disjunctive syllogism (P ∨ Q, ¬P ⊢ Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also conjunction introduction/elimination and addition: from P and Q infer P∧Q; from P∧Q infer P (or Q); from P infer P∨Q. Use truth tables to justify these patterns if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of internalizing truth tables and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should memorize and internalize truth tables for ∧, ∨, ¬, ⇒, ⇔, as these form the background language of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these symbols aids parsing mathematical sentences, constructing proofs, and avoiding ambiguity in statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle for counting lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If constructing a list of length n where there are a1 choices for position 1, a2 for position 2, ..., an for position n, then the total number of lists is a1 · a2 · ... · an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with constructing length-3 lists by branching diagram (3·2·2 = 12). Apply when choices for entries are independent and order matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists vs sets (order and repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence where order matters and repetitions are allowed; equality of lists requires same entries in same order; the empty list () has length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to confuse lists with sets: sets disregard order and duplicates. Examples and warnings about sloppy notation (omitting commas/parentheses) are given.
